name: DIRA (deficiency of the IL-1 receptor antagonist)
aliases: deficiency of the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist
neonatal-onset pustulosis with sterile multifocal osteomyelitis

reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A recessively inherited monogenic autoinflammatory disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in IL1RN, which encodes the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist
Presents in the neonatal period with pustular skin eruption, painful bone swelling, and systemic inflammation, typically without high spiking fever
The hallmark is sterile multifocal osteomyelitis with periosteal reaction, often affecting the ribs and long bones, alongside widespread pustulosis
Radiographs may show balloon-like widening of anterior ribs, multifocal osteolytic lesions, and periosteal new bone formation
Inflammatory markers are markedly elevated but blood and bone cultures are sterile, reflecting an autoinflammatory rather than infective process
Responds strikingly to interleukin-1 blockade, which replaces the missing antagonist and rapidly controls skin and bone disease
Untreated disease can be fatal in infancy from systemic inflammatory complications, so early recognition is critical
reference.pathophysiology: DIRA arises from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in IL1RN, the gene encoding the naturally occurring interleukin-1 receptor antagonist. Without this antagonist, interleukin-1 alpha and beta signal unopposed through the IL-1 receptor, driving unchecked activation of neutrophils and pro-inflammatory pathways. The resulting excess of IL-1 signalling produces sterile neutrophilic inflammation in skin and bone, manifesting as pustulosis and multifocal osteomyelitis with periosteal reaction. Because the defect lies in a soluble regulatory protein, pharmacological IL-1 blockade effectively substitutes for the missing brake and reverses the disease.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal sepsis with disseminated infection and osteomyelitis
Langerhans cell histiocytosis with bony involvement
Incontinentia pigmenti and other neonatal pustular dermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for biallelic IL1RN mutations to confirm the diagnosis
Acute-phase reactants (C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate) which are markedly raised
Skeletal survey or targeted radiographs for multifocal osteolytic lesions and periosteal reaction
Blood and bone cultures to demonstrate sterility and exclude infection
Skin biopsy showing neutrophilic pustular infiltrate
Bone biopsy where infection cannot otherwise be excluded
redFlags: Overwhelming systemic inflammation in a neonate with respiratory compromise
Extensive multifocal bone involvement causing pathological fracture or deformity
Failure to thrive with unremitting inflammation despite antibiotics
Life-threatening vasculitis or thrombosis complicating severe inflammation
reference.prognosis: Untreated DIRA carries a high risk of death in infancy from systemic inflammation, but sustained interleukin-1 blockade generally induces durable remission of skin and bone disease with a good long-term outlook.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the sterile bone and skin lesions as infective osteomyelitis and pursuing prolonged antibiotics
Delaying genetic testing and targeted IL-1 blockade while awaiting cultures
Underestimating disease severity because high spiking fever may be absent
Attributing the pustular rash to neonatal infection or common dermatoses
management: Interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra, a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist that replaces the missing protein, as the definitive therapy, with longer-acting agents such as canakinumab as alternatives
Early initiation to control neonatal pustulosis and multifocal sterile osteomyelitis and to prevent death from systemic inflammation
Supportive care with analgesia for bone pain and skin care for the pustular eruption
Exclude infection through sterile blood and bone cultures before and during immunomodulation, with ongoing vigilance for infection on biologic therapy
Monitor inflammatory markers, growth and treatment response, adjusting therapy to maintain remission
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive IL1RN mutations
Long-term follow-up under clinical immunology or rheumatology
